subtopic: AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE
subsubtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Western Grain Stabilization Plan is correct in its intention but wrong in its practice. I appeal to the Minister of Agriculture, on behalf of thousands of prairie farmers, to make quick legislative amendments to sensitize the plan to the impact of inflation and the cost of production. We have now travelled more than four years without a pay-out. The near $1 billion that has been collected is presently not serving the investors' intentions.
Record exports of grain during the past four years have prevented a pay-out even though production costs were at an all-time high and the prices were sluggish. I am asking the Government to bring forward quickly amendments that would recognize an inflation factor, the continuing steady increase of volumes of production, and allow producers a choice of levels at which they may participate in the plan.
If the Minister holds the view that such amendments are too demanding on the legislative timetable, then I urge him to seek all-party consultation on this matter before confidence in the concept is completely eroded.
In 1978 the total operating costs for farmers in the Province of Alberta were $1.7 billion. Five years later, in 1983, their operating expenses were $3.2 billion. There has not been an increase in net farm income since 1981. We must act with urgency. The need has been demonstrated.

subtopic: EDUCATION
EDUCATION
subsubtopic: UNIVERSITY AGRICULTURAL RESEARCH-LACK OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CO-OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a lack of federal-provincial co-ordination and co-operation in areas of mutual interest can result in unnecessary duplication. This can be established in the case of our universities' spending. In particular, research capacity and capability are suffering because of inadequate and poorly targeted funding and a lack of synchronization between federal and provincial research projects. There can be no doubt about the value of research. Canadian studies have shown that with each dollar spent on agricultural research the approximate rates of return are 40 per cent in the first year for wheat, 50 per cent for malt barley, and 100 per cent for western canola.
The federal Government spent $147 million on agricultural research last year, but only $14.3 million went to support university agricultural research. This federal donation should be increased, not only for research funding but also to update equipment. University budgets are insufficient to maintain equipment and facilities to produce our future scientists, and at the same time our federal Department is putting money into new facilities and equipment at its own research stations. One must ask why more co-ordination cannot be accomplished to make sure agricultural research continues with both priorities honoured. At the same time common usage of facilities could be made possible, by building government research centres on university campuses whenever possible.

February 1, 1984

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: HUMAN RIGHTS
subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next year human rights experts from around the world will meet in Ottawa for a meeting on human rights. This meeting will review the track records on human rights of the participating states to the Helsinki Accords, and will further seek to reduce the wide differences and the misunderstandings which trouble relations between East and West. This experts' meeting is required in order to further the dialogue and commentary on human rights in other participating states if we hope to persuade them to conform to international law and their commitments under the Helsinki Final Act.
Given that many of the world problems have intensified since last year, the need for an international dialogue on human rights has never been greater. I believe that it is now time for Canada to move from high sounding generalities, on which we can all agree, to specific measures for strengthening human rights guarantees. As chairman of the all-party Canadian Parliamentary Helsinki group, I recommend the establishment of an all-party special parliamentary committee or task force on human rights. Such a committee could tackle the task of preparing Canadians for the 1985 meeting of experts on human rights.

subtopic: RAILWAYS
RAILWAYS
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TECHNOLOGICAL CHANGE ON EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, technological change brings with it new challenges and new problems, as well as new opportunities. Too often, however, Canadians find themselves in the position of hearing about the opportunities first and the problems later. We hear about the predicted increase in productivity first, and the consequences for work place safety and health, or even public safety, long after, not to mention the problem of individual job loss and reduced employment levels.
One of the sectors in which this is a concern is the railway sector, and I call on the Government to pay more attention to the long-term consequences of the technological changes now being planned by the railways, the intended reduction of crews, abolition of cabooses, lengthening of trains, automation of running yards and abandonment of divisional points such as Nakina, among other things, all have probably negative public and work place safety effects, as well as having an effect on employment and the economic conditions of the individuals and the communities concerned.
Technological change must be regarded less as something inevitable with which we all have to live, and more as a series of options which are open to public debate and reflection about their over-all value, and to negotiation with those affected, as opposed to being left to private, corporate or bureaucratic imperatives.

subtopic: THE SENATE
THE SENATE
subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED NINE-YEAR TERMS FOR ELECTED SENATORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to comment upon the joint Senate and House of Commons report on Senate reform, which was tabled yesterday. The committee was reacting to the justifiable contempt in which the present Senate is held. Due to this public perception of our second Chamber, the committee has recommended a new, elected assembly. However, by insisting upon long nine-year terms of office for new Senators, the committee has denied any democratic control of the Senate. By allowing Senators to retain their seats for nine years, they become immune from the "agony" of being answerable to the electorate. Any definition of democracy includes the necessity for elected officials to be responsible to those they represent. A long nine-year term makes this impossible.
In addition, the committee has proposed that Senators would not be eligible for re-election. By this double-barrelled device of a long and unrenewable tenure of office, the public are denied the possibility of ever holding their elected representatives accountable for their actions.
In any other nation this proposed reform of the Senate would be considered a backward step, a body blow to the very workings of a democratic society. Canadians must not let their revulsion of the present decaying creature we call the Senate lead them into accepting the unacceptable.

subtopic: BANK OF CANADA
BANK OF CANADA
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO SUBSTITUTE AMERICAN COTTON FOR CANADIAN FLAX IN BANKNOTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recovery of the economy in Canada is a worthy objective. More investment, creating more jobs, will be an essential part of any recovery, but keeping the jobs we now have is equally vitally important. Government Departments, including Crown corporations, should be in the forefront in retaining the jobs of Canadians.
For years the Bank of Canada has used flax fibre in making our paper currency, but now the Bank of Canada is planning to substitute cotton waste for flax fibres. Flax straw and flax fibres are readily available in Canada, where flax fibre is gathered and processed by fine paper companies. Because
Oral Questions
Domtar is phasing out its decorticating operation in western Canada is no reason for the Bank of Canada to eliminate flax and substitute cotton from the U.S.A.
Canadian paper currency is superior to U.S. paper currency where 100 per cent cotton fibre is used; flax fibre makes the better quality. The major principle is that Canadian manufacturers of our currency should continue to use Canadian raw materials to the greatest possible degree.
Flax is grown in Canada and provides jobs for Canadians; cotton is grown in the United States and provides jobs for Americans. I want to urge the Canadian Government to insist that the Bank of Canada continue to use flax in making our paper currency.
The creation of new jobs, added to the jobs we already have and keep, will be important factors in the recovery of our economy.

EMPLOYMENT STATISTICS IN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

United States employment today is 1,845,000 higher than the pre-recession peak. In Canada it is 146,000 below. In the latest six months, Canadian employment has increased 1.4 per cent. In the United States it is up 2.3 per cent, about 50 per cent higher.
National income in the United States is 1.8 per cent higher than the pre-recession peak. In Canada, the national income is down 1.2 per cent. Industrial production in the United States in the last 12 months is up 16 per cent. In Canada it is up 6 per cent. The Canadian unemployment rate at the depth of the recession was 2 per cent higher than the United States. It is now 2.9 per cent higher.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am, of course, responsible for the effective operation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That includes the requirement that they abide by the law and by all of the operating policies within the RCMP. That I do, and I account for that to this House. speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: INSPECTION PROCEDURES FOR IMPORTED CLOTHING
speechtext:
1.
Yes, the Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, did change its inspection procedures for imported clothing.
(a)	Only specially trained Customs inspectors will examine and release clothing shipments.
February 1, 1984

(b)	The examinations were made more detailed and thorough because of complaints from Canadian clothing manufacturers that many importations did not meet the Canadian marking, labelling and import permit requirements.
(c)	The Cabinet authorized these changes.
(d)	The examinations began on August 8, 1983 and are continuing.
(e)	The program has cost approximately $100,000 from August 8, 1983 to December 31, 1983.
2.	The Government is aware of some unusual delays that occurred at the beginning of the program.
(a)	The following program changes were made to preclude unreasonable delays:
(i)	Importer profiles showing results of examinations were used to effect more selective examinations. This reduced the number of examinations required.
(ii)	Inspectors in large centres were re-deployed to where volumes were highest (example, certain airports have a particularly heavy number of shipments).
(iii)	Priorities were established to concentrate on major shipments and on those where existing control of permits because of quota arrangements necessitated more detailed verification.
(iv)	Importation of samples for production or sale were excluded from the increased surveillance procedures except that their examination and release were handled only by the specially trained officers.
(v)	Additional officers were trained to replace and, if necessary, augment the present group. Overtime was authorized when necessary.
(vi)	Shipments requiring labelling changes were released to the importers on the understanding that new or amended labels would be affixed before the goods were displayed for sale.
(b)	There were various reasons for delays, many of which were beyond the control of the Government. The majority of delays was due to the increased number of examinations required and the unexpected high rate of non-compliance with existing marking, labelling and import permit requirements detected by the examining inspectors. However, when the previously mentioned procedures were implemented, 11 days into the program, unusual delays were eliminated.
(c)	There was no shortage of inspectors, however, in some regions it was necessary to add additional personnel to ensure against unreasonable delays due to inspector illness or absence.
(d)	Clothing inspectors are situated at the major ports of entry and travel to smaller ports as required. The requirement to travel to examine shipments does on occasion take longer than if local inspectors did the releasing. The travel time used by the inspectors have marginally diminished the time available for inspection, however, specially trained inspectors are more efficient.
3.	No additional staff was hired to carry out the inspections.

(a)	Not applicable, (i) Not applicable, (ii) not applicable.
(b)	Regular Customs inspectors who received special training in the area of marking, labelling and import permit requirements were assigned to carry out the inspection.
(c)	There were no new inspectors.
(d)	Inspection time varies depending on the size of a shipment and if infractions are detected. For example, a full container with a value for duty of $40,000 or $50,000 will take longer to examine than a postal shipment worth $300 or $400. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, January 31, 1984, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to put on the record some remarks on Bill C-12 which is before the House. It involves an institution dear to my heart and I am sure of interest to all Members in the House and all Canadians, and that is, the Canadian university. We often think of universities as simple institutions of learning, almost of an elitist kind, meant for those children of people in Canada who can afford to pay for their university education. Indeed, many years ago that was exactly the case. Over the last number of decades universities have evolved into democratic institutions which virtually any Canadian given the capability and the capacity to absorb post-secondary education can attend and receive the benefits of a university education.
1 have said that universities are educational institutions, but they also ought to be regarded as industries. Indeed, they are industrial enterprises in the sense that they employ a great number of persons and contribute to the economy in the areas in which they are located. I can readily attest to that fact because in the City of Halifax universities are one of the major industries. We are fortunate to have in Halifax and in the surrounding area a number of well established and top notch Canadian universities, including Dalhousie University, St. Mary's University, Mount Saint Vincent University, the Technical University of Nova Scotia, as well as the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design and others. When we realize how important these institutions are, not only to our society, but to the local economy in places like Halifax and other university towns and cities in locations across Canada, we have to consider that, not only contributing to universities, we are not only supporting and helping the students who are receiving the benefits of a university education but we are also contributing to the economy of the regions. We are providing employment, we are generating activity and in the end we are receiving back those dollars we invest in universities two and threefold and more.
One might consider what the source of funds is in Canadian universities and how much is involved. I have a few statistics here that I asked to have prepared. They are truly amazing. Over $4.7 billion is spent by universities in Canada. Just to give you an idea of the enormity of the situation, Mr. Speaker, there are over 720,000 students enrolled full or part-time in Canadian universities. The number of faculties is in the area of
February 1, 1984

26,000. We are talking about a relatively massive economic force when we talk about universities, both in terms of personnel, faculties and students and in terms of a total dollar expenditure of $4.7 billion. When you consider that amount is almost 50 per cent or 60 per cent of the amount spent on national defence, you realize the enormousness of these university institutions in relation to the Canadian economy.
What is important is not just the numbers of persons in universities and dollars spent but the quality of a university education in Canada. That is the point we must always bring to the floor of the House of Commons when we are discussing expenditures in relation to Canadian universities. I am certain that all Canadians want the very best quality in university education for young Canadians. We cannot disregard the relationship of our financial investment in relation to the quality of education. We have to realize that every dollar of which we deprive universities will result in a deterioration of the quality of education in those universities. One only has to speak to university administrators to realize that this is in fact the case. We cannot, by direct action or indirect policy, deprive universities of the funds they need to operate at the level considered appropriate. The result will be reflected in the quality of education. In short, we save nothing by depriving universities of dollars, rather, we will find in every case those dollars will have to be spent in some other way. It will result in dollars being spent in areas like unemployment insurance for students who cannot get employment because they do not have the technical and other skills they might have gained in a university with a high standard of education.
There is another aspect of university funding that I want to bring to everyone's attention so we will not pretend that we are accomplishing anything by cutting back on the amount of funds paid to universities. While most of the funding in Canadian universities today comes from government sources, some comes from the private sector and, more important, some of the funding comes from the students themselves.
If the Government which contributes approximately 72.4 per cent of university funding, cuts back on the amount of that funding and reduces that percentage, there are only two sources from which that decreased funding can be recaptured. The first is the private sector, which now contributes something in the area of 16 per cent or less to universities. Second, the balance has to be obtained through tuition fees, which amount to approximately 15 per cent of university funding. There is a limit to the extent to which universities can press the private sector for funding. I think it is fair to say that they are making every effort they can to obtain funds from the private sector in the way of direct grants, subsidization of university projects, etc.
What remains is to raise funds from tuition fees. Indeed that has been happening in the last few years. Tuition fees have risen dramatically. I had a survey conducted for the academic year 1982-83 as it relates to the Province of Nova Scotia. I have a listing of the amounts of tuition between academic year 1981-82 and the subsequent academic year 1982-83. In the case of Acadia University, base tuition fees increased from
Established Programs Financing
$970 to $1,110, for a 14.4 per cent increase. That was topped by the French-language university in the southwestern part of Nova Scotia, the University of Sainte Anne, which had a 15.4 per cent increase in fees from $910 to $1,050. That range of increase of approximately 12 per cent to 15 per cent in tuition fees pertained to all Nova Scotia universities. Dalhousie University, Mount Saint Vincent University, St. Francis Xavier, St. Mary's University, the Technical University of Nova Scotia, the University College of Cape Breton, University of King's College, in addition to Acadia University and the University of Sainte Anne, had increases in tuition fees of between 12 per cent and 15 per cent.
When we consider that in relation to the Government's undertaking to keep increases in the proximity of the six and five program, we realize what a fraud that program was on Canadian universities and particularly on university students. The whole thesis of the six and five program which was introduced in June 1982 was to limit salary increases and other expenditure increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent and, in turn, have the same limit apply to the increases which would affect the beneficiaries of government expenditures, whether it was by way of salary or other forms of financial benefit. Universities and university students who were faced with 6 per cent and 5 per cent limitations on their financial support had to turn around and face increased tuition fees in the area of 12 per cent to 15 per cent. That is how the Government treats Canadian university students. I hope the 720,000 university students across Canada will take note of this and reassess their view of the Government of Canada in relation to the assistance and help which it has provided over the past few years.
I personally think that raising university funding from the student body is no longer an acceptable way to fund universities in Canada. It is right and proper that university students across the country contribute very substantially to the cost of their education. We live in the kind of society where we are all expected to make a contribution and to realize and recognize that we do not get anything for nothing. To found or base the future of our universities, their expansion and the increase in the quality of the educational system they provide, upon the ability of students to pay would be a grave mistake. It is a grave mistake not only in relation to the students who bear the direct result of the policy, but it is a grave mistake in relation to the whole country which benefits in many ways, as I have already indicated, from the institution of the Canadian university.
We have heard the Government talk time and time again about high technology being the hope for the future in terms of employment, that those Canadians who are now unemployed or underemployed have as their future hope the possibility that Canada will develop quickly and substantially in areas of high technology and will become a world class competitor in these areas and thus generate employment.
How could we possibly succeed in that endeavour if we do not give the necessary financial support to our universities? It is almost ludicrous for the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) to come into the Chamber and tell us

February 1, 1984
Established Programs Financing about the $2 billion which he has allocated for employment programs that will enable the retraining of undertrained employees, that will enable other Canadians to acquire the skills necessary to compete in a world of technology, and at the same time have the Government introduce other financial policies which have the effect of reducing the amount available to Canadian universities to carry on the programs. It is a total contradiction. The Government may be fooling some people for a certain period of time, but that kind of policy will have to come out in the end; the results will have to be known and recognized. The results will be very simple and very dramatic. We will not have Canadians trained in the way that they must be trained to carry on their obligations and compete in the world of technology.
With respect to the universities in my area, they have battled economic adversity for many years. The latest government policy which will deprive them of some of their funding or will result in a reduction in their funding will be just another millstone around the neck of local Nova Scotia universities. However, I want to underline specifically the plight of Mount Saint Vincent University which is located in my constituency of Halifax West. Of Canadian universities Mount Saint Vincent should really be in the spotlight because it is the only university in Canada which is dedicated to the education of women. It started as a university institution operated by the Sisters of Charity for a female student body. Over the years the university has changed so that the religious institution known as the Sisters of Charity is no longer the owner and operator of the university and it has become a public university. In more recent years it has been fit to admit a few men to the student body, not enough to colour the campus something other than female.
I am glad there are some women members in the House to hear what I am saying. I say to them and to all Canadian women that the Mount Saint Vincent University should be given special attention by them because it has stood for many decades as a bastion of education for women. Today it serves as a beacon in the quest of women for equal rights, not only in the human sense but in the very important economic and practical sense on a day to day basis.
As one male member of this Chamber and as one male Canadian, I can say that we are kidding ourselves if we think we have advanced the cause of women's rights to any great extent over the last decade. We have not recognized in a real or true sense the difficulties women have found particularly in the professions and, let's face it, in the areas of more economic return. Mount Saint Vincent and its faculty are more aware of this than perhaps other institutions and people in Canada. The President of that university, Dr. Margaret Fulton, has been a crusader for many years-and I hope for many more years to come-for women's rights, not in any silly way nor simply as a facade or window dressing, but by way of establishing programs and policies which will change in a real and dramatic manner economic opportunities for Canadian women.
Mount Saint Vincent has a number of programs which are designed to bring about this kind of real change. In each case
the program requires very special and specific funding. It is not the kind of dollars which can be raised from the student body in the form of tuition fees. It is virtually impossible to obtain this kind of funding from the private sector, so the university has to look to government. I am very sad that in so many cases individuals, institutions and businesses have to look to the Government of Canada, but in a country where so many of our dollars are taken away in the form of taxation, it becomes a necessity.
I make this appeal with that reservation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), to the extent that he controls the budget of Canada, and to the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal), to the extent that he is involved in funding for Canadian universities. They should give special attention to this tremendous and unique institution which exists in Halifax West, namely, Mount Saint Vincent University. They should take specific steps to ensure that that institution is able to fulfil the role it has undertaken over the decade so that it can be a beacon for women in Canada in a very real and practical way. It should be a place at which women have the opportunity to establish educational programs that will be of special benefit to them, a unique place in which women have the kind of control and authority that is needed to ensure that there is an evolution and development of programs that will benefit them in a real way.
On many occasions I have talked to the President of Mount Saint Vincent University, Dr. Margaret Fulton, about some of the specific programs that the university would like to found and foster. I will not elaborate, but I hope that when those in the Chamber and across Canada hear the name Mount Saint Vincent University, they will immediately recognize that it is a very special place, a place in which all Canadians, particularly Canadian women should take a special interest.
In the few minutes remaining to me, I want to repeat my plea to the Government of Canada to recognize that in its negotiations with the provinces over university funding it is dealing not only with the welfare of Canadian students, but with an educational industry that employs a great many Canadians. It is of great benefit to those areas of Canada which are fortunate to be the location for Canadian universities. We are not dealing with an isolated matter, but a matter in terms of university education that affects all Canadians. Any dollar spent in that way will benefit everybody. All Canadians should take an interest to ensure that adequate funds are provided to Canadian universities.

Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear the Hon. Member talk about the university in his constituency, Mount Saint Vincent. As he says, it is a beacon as far as the higher education of women is concerned. When the Hon. Member is urging that, and I know that he will if it is forthcoming, will he also look at the excellent women's studies programs that have been started in a dozen or so other universities in Canada? 1 know in my own most recent university where I was president, Simon Fraser started as women's studies program when 1 was there. Since he is interested and concerned about the development of education for women, will he also encourage the development of chairs in women's studies at universities that have already established women's studies programs and whose programs need to be enhanced?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of participating in the debate today. It
Established Programs Financing
is an important debate on Bill C-12 which attempts to cap the federal contribution to the provinces through the EPF program to five and six. I am particularly concerned about the effects this will have on the universities and on our young people.
There is no doubt that young people today face a crisis that has not been seen before. This is the TV generation, a generation that has a high level of expectation. They expect to be able to get an education to the fullest extent of their desire and ability. They expect to get a decent job. They expect to be able to map out their career and live a full and productive life. Perhaps they are unfortunate to be part of a baby boom that came to its maturity in a period of recession, a period when we have a Liberal Government that does not believe in forward planning, one that has no concrete thoughts of where to place the products of the baby boom or to incorporate these people into society. We have a generation coming up that is not finding any way to obtain jobs. With the Bill before us, and previous Acts brought in by the Government, the door to higher education is being shut on them.
Let us look at their opportunities for employment. In July last year, the official statistics showed an unemployment rate in this country of 1,460,000, or 12 per cent of our work force population. Of these, 290,000 or 20 per cent are under the age of 25. Twenty per cent unemployment among our young people means that one out of every five is unemployed. It is a time in their lives when they are looking for meaningful work, a time when they want to set off on their career. They cannot even start at first base. They are being shut off, Mr. Speaker. They are being shut out.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, through government policies we have a crisis in accessibility to our universities. In the last number of years there has been a continual erosion in the ability of young people to get into universities to get their degrees in order to get meaningful jobs. It is estimated that over 100,000 students have been turned away from postsecondary institutions in Ontario alone in the past two years because of the lack of space and sufficient student financial aid. The Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada is currently conducting a survey to assess the enrolment picture for this year. We do have some indication of what it is like. For example, about 56,000 students applied for 30,000 openings at Montreal's four universities. In Ontario, York University has turned away 1,400 qualified students, and 24,000 have applied to Humber College for a mere 1,000 spaces. Technical institutes in Edmonton and Calgary received 20,000 applications for a total of 10,700 spaces. The picture is complete across the country, Mr. Speaker. Over and over again we see universities having to turn students away because there are no spaces for them. The predictions of the past that university enrolments will decline as the baby boom generation goes out into the market and gets jobs are not coming true. There are no jobs for them. Many of them, and a lot of older students, are trying to get back into university to upgrade themselves in order to be able to compete for the jobs which are out there. Their ability to go back to university in order to do that is now

February 1, 1984
Established Programs Financing being diminished. The six and five program which the Government is proposing will aggravate a bad situation.
A national crisis exists for our younger people, Mr. Speaker. A generation is being wasted. A generation which was brought up full of hope and expectation is being told that there is no room for them in our society, universities or in the labour force. Where are they to go? What is to happen to this generation? Are they to be left alone on the streets with the subsequent consequences? Is this why the Government is so anxious to have a secret police in force? Does it know of the social unrest which will occur when there are more and more young people with high levels of expectation and no way to fulfil those expectations? Does it know that there will be social unrest and social tensions and that a stronger police force will be needed in order to control the anxiety and anger that will exist among those young people? Is this the Liberal solution to the problems of the young people? It is indeed sad, Mr. Speaker, to see the waste of human resources which the Government is allowing to occur and in fact, in its own stupid way, has encouraged.
There is another very important area which will suffer because of the Government's move, that is the area of social, economic and natural science research. There is no doubt that the universities play a key role in research in Canada. Without universities with proper labs, equipment, libraries and properly paid staffs, all the efforts to channel 1.5 per cent of our GNP into research will come to nought. It will not work without a strong university component in this country. Surely the backroom planners of the Government can see that. That is why I am totally flabbergasted that it has allowed legislation like Bill C-12 to proceed into the House.
We all realize, Mr. Speaker, that we are living in a rapidly changing world. There are cultural, social, economic, and technological changes. People must be prepared to meet those changes. We need research and research facilities if Canada is to play a forward role in the introduction of new technologies into our lives. In Canada most clinical medical research is done at the universities, as is most research in theoretical physics, meteorology, biology, the social sciences and culture. Universities play a vital role in research in agriculture, fishery, forestry, engineering, chemistry, economics and business administration, to name a few. They have a central position in the development and sustainment of Canadian culture. This work is both basic and applied. The Government has now expressed its concern about the lack of research in forestry. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, it is quite willing to cut further the resources which we do have within our universities to do research in forestry. What stupidity, Mr. Speaker!
It is not that the Government has not been warned. Over and over again studies, commissions and briefs presented to the Government have warned it about the need to maintain a strong research component in our universities. The Science Council of Canada in its report, University Research in Jeopardy, stated the following:
Our universities have a crucial role to play. As the site of most of our basic, and an appreciable amount of our applied research, and as the chief supplier of
the highly qualified manpower required for R&D, it is essential that they be able to maintain and improve the quality of their teaching and research. For the past ten years their ability to perform this function has been severely tested, as a result of the financial restraints imposed by federal and provincial levels of government.
If the federal Government is serious about allocating 1.5 per cent of our GNP for research and development by 1985 there could be major problems in securing the skilled manpower required to accomplish this goal. If it is going to cut the resources of the universities further, the universities will not be able to produce the trained manpower that will be needed in order to achieve that goal. Surely that should be obvious to the Government and to the bureaucrats. It escapes me why they miss the point.
I wish to read into the record the submission made by the Canadian Council of Professional Engineers in their brief to the parliamentary task force on employment opportunities for the eighties. They state the same thing as the Science Council. They state:
Adequate funding of our universities and colleges to allow replacement of equipment, expansion of facilities, and fair salaries for faculty and support staff will pay great dividends in our long-term future economic development. The graduates of those post-secondary institutions will be at the frontiers of technological and economic progress in Canada. If our educational system is allowed to deteriorate, if pure and applied research dwindle, if morale and quality of teaching drop, Canada's long-term future will suffer.
We are being warned over and over again that cutting funding to universities is done at our own peril. The economic, social, cultural and technological future of this country will suffer if the ability of the universites to participate actively in those areas is decreased. Yet the Government, in its blindness, proceeds ahead with its predetermined goals.
The crunch under which the Government has placed the universities goes back to the major cutback of 1982. At that time it decided unilaterally to change the formula in which the EPF funds were given over to the provinces. This unilateral action was a severe blow to the provincial coffers and, in turn, to the universities. What it is doing now is taking an other unilateral retroactive step-retroactive by some 18 months. How in the name of heaven can we expect the universities to do any planning when the Government, at a whim and at its own will, decides to change the formula again? How in heaven's name can we expect such important institutions as the universities to make any proper projections or do any planning if a government like the one opposite runs helter skelter, afraid for its political life and is willing to destroy all sorts of established programs and traditions in the country?
The political panic of the Government is harming all our social institutions, which in turn threatens the economic and cultural future of the country. Its political panic is threatening research projects throughout the country. Its political panic is threatening the very future of the country.
What does the Government want? What does it want from universities? It says it is not getting enough exposure, that the work it does and the moneys it pays to universities are not appreciated. If that is the problem, I am sure that the Univer-
February 1, 1984

sity of Regina would be willing to put up a big neon sign showing that the federal Government has contributed so many dollars to its operation. I am sure it would be willing to have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) present^ cheques every month or every week, if need be. But for heaven s sake, it should not disturb the programs. If it wants publicity and exposure, I am sure the University of Regina would give it if that is the price it had to pay in order to maintain its programs.
The Government is practising a type of economics very close to the Reagan type of economics. In order to meet the problems of mismanagement and deficits, it is shifting programs and responsibility over to the provinces. That is what Ronald Reagan has done in the United States.
I was interested when I heard Ronald Reagan announce on television that he is going to run again. The Governor of New York State was also interviewed and he was not too happy with Mr. Ronald Reagan and his economic policies. He said that since Mr. Ronald Reagan came to power, programs have been cut and, as a consequence, the State of New York has had to find millions of dollars in order to provide homes for the homeless. It has had to find hundreds of millions of dollars in order to find food for welfare recipients in the State of New York. In the United States, responsibilities and expenses have been shifted from the federal level to the state level.
That is exactly what the jokers opposite are doing here today. It is as unacceptable in the United States as it is in Canada. We have the same type of Reagan economics. What suffers are the universities, programs like medicare and assistance programs to the poor and disabled. The federal Government intends to shift its responsibility for those institutions to the provinces. But Mr. Speaker, when such responsibilities are given to the provinces, then the country does not have a uniform system. Poorer provinces cannot afford to maintain the same type of facilities and offer the same type of educational opportunities to their young people as other provinces. Of course, the poorer provinces and poorer regions will suffer. The Maritimes already have great difficulty keeping their bright young people, so this is a further blow to their culture and their ability to retain them. Now their universities will not be able to offer the same type of resources as the universities in Montreal or Toronto so their bright young people will have to leave in order to get an education.
That will be the result of the moves that the Government will perpetuate with Bill C-12. There will not be an equal opportunity for young people to get a good education in any part of the country.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in today's debate on Bill C-12. I recall on Thursday, April 1, 1982, participating in a similar debate around the focus of federal involvement in university funding. In that debate I found from Members on the Government benches a total rejection of the question of what is our understanding and philosophy regarding university and post-secondary education in Canada and what we expect for the future. The Bill at that time was Bill C-97. Today we have Bill C-12, entitled an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977. This, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, is a revealing title. Were it not for the conventional necessity of labelling Bills in what we could call "high toned legalese", this legislation might more reasonably be entitled something like "an Act to break all existing agreements with the Canadian people on the future of post-secondary education in Canada". Instead of trotting out reams of self-serving nonsense about the MacEachen memorial on the six and five mythology, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) would have better spent the time of the House by submitting an apology, I suggest, in the name of the current Government for lending his name to an attempt to save $380 million for the federal Treasury over two years at the expense of post-secondary education in Canada.
With all the examples of the idiotic and ridiculous use of public funds which have filled the reports of successive Auditors General through the years, why in the name of common sense, Canadians are asking, even for the sake of political expediency, would this regime decide to "save money" in the single most valuable area of Canada's economic and social growth? This leaves many people breathless, because the Government is suggesting through its other Departments and agencies, whether it be in the areas of agriculture or medical research or other fields, that we have to be on the cutting edge through these resources.
My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), have laid out the hidden agenda of this legislation in dramatic economic terms. The public is listening very carefully to their exposure of the grisly, damaging chain of events which the passage of Bill C-12 would trigger. In my role as Opposition critic of the Department of the Secretary of State-that Ministry charged with the transfer of post-secondary educational support-I would like to address in the moments given to me today another "hidden agenda" which, like it or not, this legislation includes. This
hidden agenda should be ultimately recognized for what it is, a concerted effort by the central Government of Canada to limit the potential growth and development of all Canadians through reduced support to higher levels of education.
I would like to refer Hon. Members to the most recent annual report issued by the Department of the Secretary of State. The annual report for 1982-83, under the educational support program, refers to Article 24(3) of the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, the very Act that Bill C-12 is aimed at undermining. I quote, Mr. Speaker, from page 29 as follows:
-the Secretary of State shall, as an essential and continuing indication of the interest of the Government of Canada ... consult with the governments of the provinces with regard to the relationship between the programs and activities of the governments of Canada and of the provinces that relate to post-secondary education.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that what we have in front of us today is a unilateral, confrontational move by the federal Government, not only to save money, but to shirk responsibilities for education support, which date from the Rowell-Sirois Report, which were underlined in the report of the Massey Commission and which are laid out, under the heading of "General Support and Education Opportunity Objectives", on page 36 of the annual report of the Secretary of State.
Successive Secretaries of State have been quick to accuse the provincial Governments of underfunding post-secondary institutions. They have been equally quick to accuse everyone from students to faculty to administrators of misappropriating education support funds. This is nonsense. An accountable dollar spent on opening educational opportunities will always be rewarded threefold. That should be the guiding objective behind any negotiations with the provinces, not greater federal visibility-greater accessibility, not a grab for the federal Treasury. Yet we listen to endless complaints from the federal Government about things not being done according to the agreement. What is its response? It introduces a proposal to break all previous agreements. Does the federal Government take the high road and provide a direction of leadership in resolving admittedly difficult negotiations with the provincial Governments? Certainly not. That is not the tradition of this Government. It goes into a six and five snit and enshrines its childishness in Bill C-12. Despite the recommendations of the Auditor General of federal research funding agencies and of university faculties and students, the federal Government slaps six and five on its support of post-secondary education, instead of making a move to reduce the duplication of its efforts in conducting research within so many different government Departments.
This Government's first inclination is to blame everyone else but itself for the current state of affairs. The question surely is, where is the leadership? During times of long overdue restraint on public spending, does it not occur to the federal Government to move more of its in-house research and language training needs out to the universities in lieu of some support dollars? I see no evidence of that. It might actually result in the federal Government's receiving some innovative research advice years before a trend of events hamstrings its policy
February 1, 1984

options. There is a lot to be said for supporting a research capacity which offers long-term courses of action for avoiding national dilemmas.
I will deal for a moment with an aspect of this legislation which the Government has apparently not considered. I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the submission of the YMCAs of Canada to the Macdonald Commission. That submission addresses itself to the development, "... of a holistic view of community and international development. A long-term economic plan is limited without equally strong social accountability". What 1 hear the YMCA saying is that a country must have a clear strategy for social and economic development, based on a well educated opinion of its public. The submission of the YMCA goes on to quote from Willis Harman's book, "Optimistic Outlooks", wherein he observes four major positive responses to our current situation. First of all, he cites the ecological outlook, a concern for environmental protection, resource conservation, wilderness preservation and the fostering of wholesome relationships between mankind and nature. Secondly, he cites appropriate technology, focusing on relationships between people and technology, emphasizing the use of small, decentralized technology under the control of the user that does not cause undue insult to the environment and is compatible with a voluntarily simple lifestyle. He then goes on to talk about personal liberation, emphasizing development of self-reliance and self-emancipation from prejudice and stereotypes relating to race and sex, from oppression by patriarchal societal institutions and from the dehumanizing effects of the giant organizations of industrial society. Fourthly, he speaks about spiritual revitalization, emphasizing the research for meaning and value, renewed attention to the spiritual, and release of human potential.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you and Members of the House as well as Members of the public who follow the debates here will see my point. When the federal Government decides to take the unthinking route of limiting its support to post-secondary education, it does the whole country a disservice. At the same time it undercuts some of its own initiatives in other fields. For example, it launches an investigation into visible minorities, but limits support of the very tool which gives the lie to racism. For example, it asks the country to support the exploration of the North, but limits support for education which allows people affected to make well educated responses. It limits its support for the humanities and educational opportunities to develop social values, yet asks Canadians to support it in such crucial initiatives as changing the divorce law, introducing national security service legislation, and the creation of multicultural ministries of Government. On it goes.
This Bill breaks more than an agreement with provincial governments. I suggest that it breaks a trust with the Canadian people. In its submission to the Macdonald Commission, the Canadian Association of University Teachers spoke of a funding crisis in the universities. Current levels of funding are inadequate to meet national goals similar to those of our major competitors. Yet both levels of Government have decreased
Established Programs Financing their commitment to fund higher education. The result is a steady decline in the quality of scientific equipment and libraries, and a serious loss of morale on the part of professors. This crisis must be addressed by proper funding by both levels of government, and by an end to the destructive and mindless quarrel between the federal Government and the provinces over joint funding mechanisms. As we move into the twenty-first century, how we deal with our universities, their faculties and students, will in large measure determine Canada's position in the next century.
I want to suggest to the Minister that in his opening comments in this debate he said the federal Government decides from time to time how best to allocate the huge sums for training and educating our young people. From experience in my own riding with the Universities of Waterloo and Wilfrid Laurier University, the Conestoga Community College and the neighbouring University of Guelph, I know the predicament of many young people and the need for providing greater access to university, particularly at a time when these young people cannot find work. In many cases we are going to be assisting them through unemployment insurance or other social measures. But the question of why we are starving the universities and the question of the implications, as I hear them in my own riding and on the national scene, has long range effects. We are losing world class scholars, and these do not come back with an up-turned economy. We are finding now that there is no place for many of our qualified academics, and as a result we are losing a generation of highly educated young people. As we freeze and cut back in university departments, those who have tenure stay on and many of our finest young men and women cannot find a teaching position. Then of course we are increasingly making universities elitist as we put a higher and higher price tag on entry for students who have no jobs.
Why, Mr. Speaker, does the Government announce that over the next five years it will spend in the neighbourhood of $3 million to $4 million for women's Outreach programs while at the same time it is trying in this Bill to cut back $380 million in universities? Instead of porkbarreling those funds into an election campaign, why not put them into the universities where programs to enhance the role of women can be developed?
My colleague from Halifax West spoke about Mount St. Vincent. There are unique opportunities there to think through carefully to develop a plan for training and retraining of women and for breaking many of the social taboos. On the one hand Government cuts back funding to universities and on the other it increases the staff of an agency such as CIDA to develop international assistance programs. Here we have internationalized institutions, audited in a way that could be quite satisfactory to the Auditor General, able to administer effectively our international development assistance, and they are all but ignored by a growing bureaucracy in Hull. Why is it that some of the best administrative machinery and some of the most knowledgeable people are not engaged in this work,

February 1, 1984
Established Programs Financing
and the establishment of CIDA then reduced to a small overall monitoring group?
When we begin to look at the expenditures in environmental ministries, cultural necessities, medical research and all the dollars now being wasted or directed to other areas, why is it that we are so short-sighted that we cannot see that the place which can provide the resource, a publicly funded institution, is not maintained? Why do we not rationalize it in such a way that pure research and directed research can be carried out and we can move through this period with that national resource in place for the future? In terms of research and development, the cutting edge, there are reports upon reports, including reports from Ministers of this Government, which indicate that the investment must be in research and development and innovation. On the one hand the Government puts money into innovation centres and on the other it starves the institution in which it set up the innovation centre. Many Canadians are asking: Does the right hand know what the left hand is doing? In the same way, Revenue Canada on the one hand attacks small businesses and on the other the Minister of Finance says that we must have policies to encourage small businesses.
With a Government in disarray, the question before Canadians in this House is: How can we vote for a Bill which quite clearly indicates that there is no national policy for renewal, there is no rationalization of existing resources?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have mixed feelings in rising to speak in this debate. While the subject may be abstract for some, it is not so for the people in my community. For the second time in seven years we are faced with seeing a provincial government not only cutting back on post-secondary education in my district, but wiping out a university totally for the second time. We were advised only a couple of weeks ago that as of May 1 the David Thompson University Centre in the City of Nelson will no longer exist. It being May Day, I do not know if the date has any significance, given the author of the action to which I am referring. This action is enough to make those of us who live in our community bitter. People in our community not only care about providing post-secondary education for people in our riding but also for providing one option for post-second ary education outside of the lower mainland of our province, the lower section of Vancouver Island and the major metropolitan areas so that people would have some choice as to the type of education available and the option of pursuing that education at a location somewhat closer than 500 miles from home.
In 1977 a provincial government of the same stripe as the one under which we suffer today took exactly the same kind of action against a university which existed on the same site. The present institution is not large. There are approximately 500 students and 100 faculty and staff. When one considers the impact this will have not only on the faculty, on other staff and
on students of the university centre but also the economic impact it will have in a city of slightly under 10,000 people, it is an action tantamount to the murder of a community. It is the second time it has happened in just seven years.
You will probably appreciate from these remarks that I have received significant communications from a number of my constituents and interested parties in my area and throughout British Columbia since these announcements were made. In order to give the Government an understanding of the consequences of the B.C. Government's total reneging on its commitments, let me quote from an editorial that appeared in the Trial Times on January 6, under the heading "No One Surprised". It reads:
The word surprise does not comply with its definition when applied to the Wednesday afternoon announcement from Victoria by Education Minister Jack Heinrich that the provincial government will close Nelson's David Thompson University Centre in May.
The brief press release, handed out by a government flack, said in these tough times the money is not warranted invested in education in the Interior, and tough as it may prove to be, DTUC must close.
There are a number of reasons why this devastating announcement for Nelson is not surprising. The content and nature of the statement reflect clearly-established Social Credit practices. They include blaming any cost-cutting on a need for spending restraint, giving education short shrift in a government philosophy for its citizens' basic needs and well-refined insensitivity to the people it represents and whose lives it affects.
DTUC campus director Richard Pearce, like almost all his colleagues and students, stumbled on to the bad news about the May 1 closure by listening to Nelson radio station CKKC. Selkirk College principal Leo Perra-
They are jointly responsible for the administration of the university centre.
-tried to phone the news to Pearce-
The head of DTUC.
-from Victoria, but could not reach him.
Pearce and others are caught off-guard because just over three months ago Heinrich and Universities Minister Pat McGeer were reassuring DTUC officials that provincial money would continue to support the school. Suddenly, a late afternoon radio story took the truth out of their promises.
What we have here in terms of the impact of cut-backs in post-secondary education in a community is not only vicious but an action that was launched in a surprise attack, one which, while on a different scale, is akin to the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour. This took place after two Ministers of that Government gave commitments just months before and following direct commitments made by the Premier of that province in that same town seven years previously when the government set up a new university after scrapping the previous one. At that time, the entire academic and surrounding communities were put through the gut-wrenching turmoil of having to see all those jobs disappear and then going through the reconstruction of an institution and the community from scratch. Between 1972 and 1975 there were 800 students. That number declined to nothing and was slowly built back up to 500 students in a brand new institution. It is a bit much to ask any community to bear that burden again.
I want to do more than just talk about what the Government of British Columbia has done.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with all respect, if I had not thought that the connection was so obvious, perhaps I would have explained it more explicitly. Of course, as one who is in the midst of the situation it may appear more obvious to me than it does to others.
As a result of the federal Government's moving to block funding in 1977, it did to post-secondary education in many ways that it allowed to happen with regard to the cutbacks in the medicare, health insurance and hospital insurance fields across the country. The Government was warned and should have known that while it has been increasing the sums of money over the years, if it simply handed that money to provincial governments, which have often acted in this way when given the opportunity, we would see exactly the devastating results that we are seeing.
In the case of British Columbia, Ottawa now contributes approximately 80 per cent of the $300 million annual cost of post-secondary education in that province. In 1983-84, the Ottawa contribution to British Columbia increased by some 7 per cent while B.C. spending went down by approximately 6 per cent. In the 1977-78 fiscal year, at the time block funding came into being, the federal transfer to B.C. in a specially earmarked fund for post-secondary education was $202 million, while in the 1983-84 fiscal year it became $451 million. The percentage of assistance from Ottawa to Victoria for the purposes of post-secondary education rose by 123 per cent, at a time when inflation in that period went up only by 72.6 per cent.
Nobody is suggesting that there have not been additional funds. Surely the federal Government knows now, watching the record of almost every provincial Government in Canada, that if we are to keep post-secondary education alive and well or to restore it to some sense of health, then rather than diverting parts of that federal funding off to other programs, whether short-term employment programs or whatever, that money should be set aside in some kind of special emergency fund because of this emergency situation. It should then be allocated in some way in order to keep institutions and programs alive, to allow students to continue learning, especially when those same students are attempting in ever greater numbers to get into post-secondary educational institutions because direct employment opportunities are not now open to them.
Established Programs Financing
A few days ago I wrote to the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) asking him to consider just such possibilities. Referring to the closure of the university in my own area, I asked him:
-to explore the possibility of the federal Government bringing economic sanctions to bear upon the provincial Government of British Columbia on the strength of federal transfer payments allotted to B.C. for education and ... further indicate to me any and all pressures that the Government of Canada may have within its power to bring about a reversal of this decision.
We are one small community, Mr. Speaker. It is perhaps a more aggravated situation than is taking place in other universities and other campuses across Canada. If we look at the impact on those students and on that faculty, it is just a microcosm of the devastating effect of the provincial Government's actions, aided and abetted by the unconditional approach which the federal Government is taking toward our young people and our future as a nation. While B.C. may be the worst case, it is not the only one. Education means more than just opportunities for a few individuals, important as that may be; it is vitally important for the fabric of our communities and the fabric of our cultural lives.
I would like in the moments remaining to me to read briefly from some correspondence I have received. This correspondence perhaps gives more weight than I can to the type of feelings that abound. First, I have a letter from a group of high school teachers in a community not far from the City of Nelson. It reads:
The decision to close down DTUC is one which must cause educators within the public school system some concern.
The community at large loses opportunities for high school graduates to continue their education close to home. A large urban university often presents a difficult adjustment for students from smaller schools; for others, the expenses become prohibitive-
Teachers in rural areas who have graduated from the special programs in the Education faculty owe their success to the presence of the university. The rural education benefits from skills that such teachers bring to their tasks.
There are specific programs, not only in the Kootenay School of Art but in specific types of rural based education programs that simply are not available elsewhere.
Another letter which touched me was from the President and Directors of the Nelson and District Arts Council. This letter is directed to the Premier of British Columbia and it reads:
We, the Directors of the Nelson and District Arts Council, ask you to change your Government's decision to close the David Thompson University Centre.
We do not ask you to restore DTUC only because we need it. Our civic and government leaders have pointed out with force and the validity of figures the economic and social blow to our community. But we ask you to restore it because the Province needs the contribution DTUC makes to our cultural life.
Thirty-two years of having a University and an Art School have made Nelson "different" from other communities; the large number of scholars and literary and fine artists and enthusiasts who live here have made Nelson a fountain head from which have come scholars, teachers, and artists, graduates and associates of DTUC and its predecessor, Notre Dame University, who are now living in communities throughout the province, and vivifying them with the spirit absorbed here-a spirit that asserts that culture is measured not in numbers but in individuals who can change the quality of life.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, let me emphasize what I think is the most telling remark in this piece of correspondence. It is:

Established Programs Financing
Even Iron Curtain countries beef up their cultural life in hard times, knowing that the economic life will survive if the people have spirit. True cost efficiency includes provision for spiritual well-being.
Surely in a society that believes in liberal values, that cherishes the human spirit as western societies presumably have traditionally done we should understand that education is more than training somebody to earn bucks in the future, that having an educated population we are imbued with some spirit of toleration and broad knowledge makes it incumbent upon all of us to attempt to keep the basis of this system, namely post-secondary education, alive. In this way we can appreciate each other for our differences as well as for those things that make us similar. We are destroying more here than simply the lives of students, the lives of faculty members and the lives of communities; we are destroying the heart and soul of our society. If this federal Government thinks it can use as an excuse the fact that we have some reactionary, conservative, regressive governments spread out across most of the provincial administrations in Canada to enable other departments to raid this budget to fill their own coffers for their own political purposes, then the Government is dangerously wrong. This action will come back to bite society in ways that none of us want to see. I hope that the Government will reconsider the action it is taking and will use the opportunity provided to put these curtailed funds back into some special emergency fund so we can ensure that post-secondary education across Canada is restored and remains alive and well.

Mr. Speaker, in the case of a community such as my own, it will immediately affect the employment of some faculty and staff. What else it might do, particularly in an area where we have seen some of our traditional resource based industries decline again because of direct policies emanating from our provincial capital, is that it will destroy interrelationship within the community which encloses it.
Even though it is my home town, 1 do not think I am overstating the fact that it is rather unique. To have that kind of microcosm of society in a
town of some 10,000 souls is unique. Because that community is somewhat isolated from the mainstream, being in the high mountains of the West Kootenays, we have built a very special kind of relationship with each other with a strong sense of family ties and a strong sense of community even as a political constituency. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with a number of items in the Bill, but 1 will start by reviewing what took place in the past in connection with medicare. In the beginning many provinces had medicare systems. Certainly Alberta had an excellent one operated by the doctors themselves. It was called MSI.
Then the federal Government came to the provinces and said that it would like to introduce a national scheme of medicare and that it would undertake to pay 50 per cent of the costs of each province which came into the agreement. This was a tempting offer for the provinces. As a matter of fact, some concern was expressed around the Cabinet table in Alberta because we had an excellent medicare system which was operating as a private enterprise system and the people liked it. The deciding factor was that we would lose the grants for health unless we did away with MSI and took medicare. The decision of the provincial government at that time was to enter into medicare on the understanding that 50 per cent of its costs would be paid by the federal authority.
That went on for a few years and the people were reasonably happy with medicare until about 1977 when the federal Government decided that it would introduce what it called block funding. Block funding might be called something different; we could call it lump sums. However, when the provinces were discussing the matter of block funding, it was never suggested to them that the total sum would be reduced. I do not know about the House of Commons but I imagine the same thing was presented here-that instead of having individual grants for medicare, education, et cetera, it would all be put into one lump sum and given to the provinces. Since they could use some discretion in the method of spending it, it had some attraction for provincial governments. They would not have the federal Government looking over their shoulders. They could use the funding in ways that would bring the best results. As far as I know all provinces agreed to it and, again as far as I know, the Conservative Opposition in the House of Commons agreed to it and the NDP Opposition opposed it.
The cry now is that when the matter was being discussed there was no suggestion that there would be some reduction in the amount of money. The various items were to be totalled and they would receive a block sum or a lump sum. This has advantages even in the area of hospitalization. If we compare 12-bed or 24-bed hospitals with larger hospitals in Montreal, Edmonton or Calgary which have tremendous services, obvi-
February 1, 1984

ously increased services will cost more. Obviously the per capita cost of large hospitals will be greater than that of small localized hospitals which provide a good and efficient service but a limited one to the people. The provinces went along with the block funding on the understanding that there would not be any reduction in the total amount.
Then we come to the next stage where we have Bill C-12. It goes a step further-the funding will be unilaterally decided by the federal Government.
Let us look at the progression. First there was an agreement. After all, hospitals and medicare are provincial responsibilities under the BNA Act. The federal Government went to the provinces and obtained an agreement so that it could properly get into the field, and there was nothing wrong with that. When that was going well, the Government introduced block funding in which it gradually reduced the amount of money which the provinces were receiving under the individual items. That became a rather vexatious matter for many provinces, perhaps all of them. Then we come to the next step where the federal Government takes over and unilaterally decides how much money would go to the medicare system.
I am not a lawyer, but it seems to me that this is a case where the federal Government is using legislation to initiate a program in which it really has no authority. Surely the agreement prior to 1977 did not give universal, all-time agreement for the federal Government to be in health care. The agreement was changed. It moved from that to block funding where it made some reductions. Perhaps they were palatable but they were reductions. Now, seven years later, we get a Bill under which the federal Government actually takes over the system.
Does the Government have the legal right to do this? 1 would like to hear a decision by the Supreme Court of Canada with regard to that. I do not think it has the legal right to do what is in the Bill. If it decides on a moral basis that it wants to make so much of a contribution, there is nothing wrong with that, but this is taking over the responsibility. Either the provinces accept it and like it, or they take it and not like it. But they have to follow it or be penalized. Consequently the provinces become responsible to the federal Government, not to the people who elected them. This is democratically wrong.
When Canada was formed the federal Government was a creation of the provinces. It should be responsible to the provinces. Now the case is that the provinces have become responsible to the federal Government when they should be responsible to the people who elected them, which is democracy.
I have a vague recollection of a story I read as a youngster in school about an Arab and a camel. I think it is applicable in this particular case. The Arab was in his tent and a severe cold spell or storm came up. He was in his nice, warm tent, and the camel came along and said: "It is cold out here, it is windy out here. Would you let me put my head in your tent?" The Arab said: "Okay, there is room for your head". A few minutes later the camel said: "Boss, my shoulders are becoming very cold, the wind is bothering them. Do you mind if I put my shoulders in your tent?" The Arab answered: "There is nothing wrong
Established Programs Financing with that; bring in your shoulders". Then the rear part of the camel's anatomy was getting cold. He said: "Do you mind, Mr. Boss, if I bring in my back legs?" He thought for a moment and then said: "Well, I guess it would be okay". A few minutes later he said: "Well, I have everything in except my tail, I may as well bring the rest of my body into the tent". He brought his whole body into the tent and pushed out the Arab. There was not room for both.
That is similar to what is happening in this instance. First the federal Government put in its head, then its shoulders, then the rear end and now it is the whole thing. The provinces will either be kicked out or penalized.
I do not like extra billing. I wish it was not required. If the federal Government still paid 50 per cent of the health costs, as it agreed to at the beginning of medicare, there would be no need for extra billing. Doctors could be paid a proper fee.
I do not like the idea of some of our specialists leaving this country. It will hurt all of Canada. We need the best physicians, surgeons and psychologists. We can keep them by providing an incentive for them to have a good standard of living. If we drive them away we all suffer. We need the top practitioners and surgeons all the way down the line. We want them to be happy.
I would like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) why the federal Government is now double-billing the people of Alberta. The Minister has publicly stated that the provinces must follow the rules set out by the federal Government. In spite of the BNA Act, if the provinces do not follow the rules they will be penalized. The federal Government will keep the money the people of Alberta pay. That is where the federal Government got the money; it came from Alberta. The federal Government says it will keep that money and the Alberta Government will have to double-bill for the difference. That is just as bad as, if not worse than, a doctor double billing. I do not like double billing in that case either, but that is what the federal Government is doing to the people of Alberta and those in other provinces where there is difficulty meeting health costs. The provinces are being helped by doctors billing the rich, those who can pay. Whether this is done by double billing, taxes or insurance, those who have the money will be the ones who pay.
Using Alberta as an example, those on welfare do not pay. The doctors do not double-bill them. Those with an income below a certain amount are not double-billed by the doctors. Pensioners are not double-billed. That is one advantage of an insurance scheme. With taxation, everyone who is eligible would have to pay the taxes. Those on lower income probably would not pay. That is only proper.
What irks me is that under this Bill the federal Government is unilaterally taking over health care in this country. It is driving the provinces out. It may well drive out the best physicians and surgeons or make them so unhappy that they will not do their best work.
